title: How Listening to Ocean Waves Can Predict Volcanic Eruptions
author: Jake Currie
text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementGeoscienceHow Listening to Ocean Waves Can Predict Volcanic EruptionsThe speed of the soothing sounds could spell disaster JCBy Jake Currie3:00 PM CDT on August 19, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleIn 2010, a dark cloud descended over Europe. Iceland’s Eyjafjallajökull had erupted, sending plumes of volcanic ash more than 60,000 feet in the air. Across Europe, air traffic came to a halt for a week—the largest disruption to air travel on the continent since World War II. President Barack Obama, in Ireland at the time, was forced to cut his European trip short, but he may have left feeling a little vindicated.Subscribe to skip adsFeatured VideoPowered By 10 How Many Black Holes Exist Across the Universe?ShareNextStayThe previous year, his administration announced a plan to spend $15 million to modernize volcano monitoring equipment, something his political opponents seized on as an example of wasteful spending. Eyjafjallajökull’s violent eruption had just demonstrated why the project was necessary. Fast forward to today, and the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) has revealed one of their new techniques to predict eruptions—listening to the ocean. As waves from the Pacific crash on the shores of the island of Hawaii, the sounds travel through the rocks. Seismometers littered around the island, typically used for listening to volcanic activity, can also pick up these gentle sounds. By measuring how quickly they travel through different parts of the island, geologists can glean useful data about how imminent a volcanic eruption is. Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
